learningObjective: Reason about MLIR Pass and PassManager semantics: op-scoping, nesting, and how a pass's op-type constrains where it runs.
stem: Which statement about MLIR PassManager and Pass scoping is correct?

options.text: The PassManager runs all registered passes in parallel by default; users must explicitly opt out of parallelism to guarantee ordering, since MLIR provides no sequential pipeline semantics.

MLIR Passes are always module-level: any pass registered with the PassManager runs exactly once on the top-level `ModuleOp`, and per-function work is achieved by having the pass walk the module manually with a `walk()` call.

Each Pass declares the Op type it runs on (e.g., `ModuleOp` or `func.func`); the PassManager runs a pass over every matching Op in the IR, and nested pass managers can be composed to run inner passes on inner ops (e.g., a `func.func` pipeline nested inside a `ModuleOp` pipeline).
Passes may freely modify any op in the IR regardless of the declared scope; the declared Op type is only a documentation hint used by the pass registry to display help text.

explanation: MLIR Passes are scoped to a specific Op type (typically `ModuleOp` or `FunctionOpInterface` / `func.func`). The PassManager iterates the pass over each matching Op in the IR. Nested pass managers allow structuring inner pipelines: e.g., a top-level `PassManager<ModuleOp>` with a nested `OpPassManager<func::FuncOp>` that runs a set of per-function passes. This nesting is the standard way to organize MLIR pipelines and to enable per-op parallel execution when opted-in.

optionExplanations.C: Correct: op-scoping and nested pass managers are the standard MLIR PassManager design.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: many passes are scoped to `func.func` directly.
optionExplanations.A: Wrong: passes run sequentially in declared order by default; parallelism across ops of the same nested level is an opt-in.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: pass scoping is a real verified constraint, not documentation.

nonImplications: Does not imply that only `ModuleOp` and `func.func` are supported scopes; user-defined op types with `OpTrait::IsIsolatedFromAbove` also work.
Does not imply passes cannot cross scope boundaries via analyses; analyses can be shared across nested managers.

distractorRationales.D: Wrong claim that scope is only a hint.
